Here's another trooper doing the exact same thing to keep people safe by time in this situation to get this car, get this resolved safely. Let's see what happens. You can see these troopers and local law enforcement. That might have been Ramsey County there, I'm not sure. stopping traffic to keep them safe. Gosh. If you're from Rochester, you'll recall from a few years ago, a very sad situation with a... Here we go, let's take a look. Now this trooper has started to catch up to the car. They did a U-turn. It took them a couple miles to finally catch up. They're going to start to take some action here. Let's see. In a typical chase, most agencies are going to limit a pit to 45 or 35 miles per hour. If they're a wrong-way driver, I don't know enough to know if other policies might come into play. You might start talking about pits at a higher speed, which would be considered lethal force, but you could see them, you know, certainly being justified in this situation. So here's our modified felony stop, gain the driver out. Right away, let's see. I've watched this several times, but each time I breathe a sigh of relief at this point, when they get the driver out successfully. Goodos to this officer climbing over the guardrail there. The last clip here is the suspect being put in the back of the car that always feels good to see. I think in this situation, it feels good to sometimes know. Justice is served. Someone is stopped. It feels good. And then seeing their car towed away. That always feels good too. So last clips to close out.
